title: JPMorgan Raises S&P 500 Target to 8,000 Saying AI Spending Is Finally Paying Off - Startup Fortune
text: JPMorgan just raised its S&P 500 target to 8,000, telling investors the AI spending boom is finally showing up in real earnings. JPMorgan strategists led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas raised the bank's year-end target for the S&P 500 to 8,000 on August 10, 2026, up from 7,800 in June and 7,600 before that. Third hike this year. The new target implies roughly 3% upside from the index's Friday close of 7,757.64. Buried in that number is a bigger claim: the trillions hyperscalers have poured into AI data centers are starting to convert into revenue you can actually see on an income statement, not just a promise on an earnings call. JPMorgan also lifted its S&P 500 earnings-per-share forecasts to $365 for 2026 and $420 for 2027, up from $350 and $390. That's not a small revision. MarketWatch reported that the bank pointed to a strong second-quarter earnings season, with 87% of S&P 500 companies already reported and nearly 80% beating earnings estimates. The bank's AI argument sits inside those numbers: Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft are seeing cloud demand and cash flow hold up, with backlogs strong enough to make the capital spending look less like blind faith and more like work already under contract. The word to watch is backlogs. A cloud backlog isn't cash in the bank, but it is better than a slide deck. If a customer has committed to future cloud capacity and that work starts turning into recognized revenue, investors get something firmer than the usual AI promise. They get sales. JPMorgan isn't alone in becoming more bullish. Goldman Sachs has also put its year-end S&P 500 target at 8,000, while Citigroup and BCA Research have been even higher in recent target updates. Reuters reported in June that at least seven research firms had raised their S&P 500 targets that month, when JPMorgan moved to 7,800. Wall Street has spent most of 2026 chasing the same adjustment: earnings estimates keep rising faster than the cautious early-year forecasts allowed. Jamie Dimon Is Personally Recruiting 40 Companies to Confront AI Risk JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon is personally phoning the heads of more than 40 major U.S. companies to join an expanded Alliance for Critical Infrastructure aimed at confronting AI risks to banks, power grids, water systems, and railroads. The outreach began in July, with discussions running through August and an eye toward coordinating with the Trump... - ai risk management for critical infrastructure - Jamie Dimon recruiting companies AI safety The spending still has to prove itself Here's the thing. The bull case rests on the idea that capex is converting into revenue fast enough to justify the spending. Plenty of analysts aren't there yet. Jefferies analysts wrote after recent tech earnings that Meta likely remained in the penalty box until investors could see clearer returns on its capital spending. Citi has also projected that Alphabet, Meta and Amazon could each run negative free cash flow in 2027 and 2028 if the AI buildout keeps climbing. That should give you pause. Nobody is saying this is 2001 again. But the basic shape is familiar enough: spend now on infrastructure, promise the revenue follows, then ask investors to wait while depreciation and financing costs pile up. Reuters recently noted that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle are expected, on current trajectories, to spend more combined on capital expenditures than they generate in free cash flow by 2027, based on LSEG consensus estimates. There is also a wrinkle in JPMorgan's own recent history that's worth sitting with. When the bank lifted its target to 7,800 in June, the same team warned that speculative, secondary and tertiary AI stocks faced flash-crash risk because trades had become crowded. Their preferred setup then was a barbell: direct AI infrastructure winners on one side and low-volatility defensive names on the other. JPMorgan hasn't walked that warning back. It's layering a more bullish earnings story on top of it. The target is not the whole trade Both points can be true. JPMorgan's 8,000 call is really about the companies selling AI compute and cloud capacity, not every stock with an AI label taped to it. Not every AI stock qualifies. Alphabet's Google Cloud backlog backs it up, and so do Microsoft's Azure demand and Amazon's AWS growth. A thin software name or hardware supplier trading only on AI excitement doesn't get the same pass. That matters more than the headline number. Readers trying to decide whether the AI trade is still investable should watch that gap, not the target itself. A bank putting a number on the S&P 500 is a forecast, not a fact. Worth remembering. But JPMorgan is now attaching hard numbers to the claim that AI capex is starting to pay for itself - real EPS revisions and a real backlog-to-revenue mechanism. The next two quarters of hyperscaler earnings will decide whether that confidence is early or earned. The target of 8,000 is JPMorgan's bet on the answer.
